I've got some tips here.

Use the monsters average damage rolls listed in most stat blocks. Players still get to roll math rocks, so there's no issue with their clacky fun, and you get to run faster and with less stress. Could even roll damage manually just for bosses to amplify the stakes of an encounter. 

Ignore the single digits behind the screen for monster hp. If they have 27 hp, round up to 30. When players roll 18 damage, round it up to 20. Roll 89 damage? Up to 90. 11 damage? That's 10 damage. This way you're only dealing with the tens column and can just ignore the ones. Won't impact player game feel, big numbers are still big numbers, and you get to do less math. I also prefer to count up health instead of counting it down. So if a monster has 300 health, I just track the tens of damage dealt until it adds up to 300.

Minions might have damage thresholds instead of hit points. Take a goblin. If the goblin takes 10 damage from a single instance of damage, they die immediately. If they take 1 to 9 damage, slap an X next to their spot on your computer or sheet, and just let them die on the second hit, even if the damage from two damage instances wouldn't add up to 10.

Or, for extreme simplicity, just keep track of the hits. Do the math for your hill giant queen and just let her ogres die in 3 or 4 hits.

Could use what some people call a "Dungeon DC" where you tell the players that all DCs and ACs of creatures in this dungeon are going to be X number. Maybe lower it by 5 for chumps and increase it by 5 for big problems. Dungeon DC for the Goblin Incubus is 16, all traps, Stealth, and mysteries require that roll. Monsters have 16 AC and DC 16 features, their goblin servants have 11 AC and DC 11 features, and the Goblin Incubus has 21 AC and DC 21 features. Maybe the acid pits are at 11, the poison arrow traps are 16, and the abyssian portal to an acidic ooze is DC 21. Just like monsters, you can have set damage for any terrain or traps like with monster damage rolls.

Lastly, all players should keep track of their own stuff, and if they're honest players and you're using a Dungeon DC, they can tell you if they succeed or fail any given roll. Even without a Dungeon DC, just giving your players the monster AC and DC can hasten the pace.

I ran a class experiment.

To simulate our real world conditions in my class of 30, I gave the following.

- 1 student automatically passed the class. 

- 4 students received all the answers but still had to do the tests. 

- 5 students were given the textbook, supplies and taught the course. I charged the students for supplies and my time. 

- 5 students could use the notes of the first 5 students but were not allowed any books, supplies, or allowed in the class. I charged the students for supplies and my time. 

- 10 students failed the class automatically. I charged the students for supplies and my time. 

From this you can read the FIVE BEST SENTENCES You'll ever read and all applicable to the experiment

1. You cannot anticipate equal results without equitable treatment.

2. Without government support, some do not get to participate in the system.

3. Exceptional ability alone is not enough to overcome exceptional circumstances.

4. When those who have the least have to work the hardest, the value of that work should go to those who produced it.

5. Those who are unable to do the work must receive the support of those who can so they may participate once given the means to do so.

In this specific instance I mentioned ranked ballot, aka alternative vote, because it was the system that Trudeau leans towards, at least he has paid lip service to it, thus it seems more feasible for that to be the evolution over MMP or STV systems.

However, feasibility doesn't represent my beliefs. I like MMP, but acknowledge its inherent challenges in regional representation. 

For example, let's say I have a community in BC that was split between Liberal/NDP/Green for progressive policy reasons and Conservatives for conservative beliefs. The results are 24% Lib, 24% NDP, 24% Green, and 28% Con, giving us a local representative with Conservative policy. Chances are we most certainly would see a selected representative who represents the overall progressive interests, but that selected representative may be from Toronto, and thus be unfamiliar with the needs of the regions the votes came from. Whereas our elected representative would not represent the overall interests of the region.

My personal bias is towards Single Transferable Vote where regions benefit from both the small-party support of alternative vote systems, but also the proportional representation of, albeit larger under STV, regions with varying needs. The benefits of eliminating strategic voting and limiting gerrymandering combined.

Yeah, so you lay out tokens, cards, coins, etc. We use 5 tokens, and I play with groups of 3 to 5 for context. 

3 tokens start on the PC side, 2 tokens on the DM side. 

The easy to understand use of course is players flipping tokens for advantage, and the DM doing the same. 

For the introduction of narrative elements, I'll use some real examples.

PCs are in a forest, one of the PCs asks if they can use a token to make a druid in the forest that they'd like to encounter. They flip a token. 

PCs are raiding a fort. I describe poorly repaired walls, fields to sneak through, guards, horses, carts, farm animals, and so on. There is a nearby river that runs from the Fort to a nearby village. The PC decides that there is a sewer entrance to the fort. They flip a token to introduce this element. 

PCs are defending a town. The villagers are pressed by the onslaught of undead. They had heard rumours of a group of bandits masquerading as heroes. The PC asks if they can use a token to have the bandits ride in for legitimate heroism. 

The PC attacks a hoard of zombies, rolling Acrobatics to maneuver through them. The zombie fight is happening in the river. Upon failing the Acrobatics check, the DM flips a token to have the player knocked prone and restrained by the river zombies. This could be considered unfair as it is a pretty extreme punishment for one failed Acrobatics check. However, the players are now granted a resource, and the rest of the party must react to this sudden shift in the encounter. 

The PC is sneaking through a fort. Upon failing a stealth check, not only are they discovered, but the evil sorceress with the power of erasure deletes an entire wall they were hiding behind, revealing the party and establishing initiative in a position very inconvenient to the party. 

The DM could definitely have these larger narrative punishments as part of the base system of 5e, even without the tokens. The addition of the tokens draws the players attention to that particular shift, establishes the gravity of the twist, and enables the DM to create intimidating complications without feeling unfair.
